content.p: On 22 March 1943 the village of Khatyn, in the forested country north of Minsk, was destroyed together with almost everyone in it. The memorial complex that now stands on the site puts the dead at 149 people, among them 75 children. The villagers were herded into a shed, the shed was set on fire, and those who burst out of the burning building were shot. The village was then looted and burned to the ground.

Khatyn was one of many Belarusian settlements wiped out in this way during the German occupation, and it became the name under which the Belarusian Communist leadership chose to commemorate hundreds of them. Two members of the 118th police battalion, Vasyl Meleshko and Hryhorii Vasiura, were tried in Soviet courts in 1975 and 1986 and sentenced to death. A third man, Vladimir Katriuk, whose name had come up at both trials, died in Canada in 2015 and, according to Laputska, was never sued for his crimes. Most of what is told about the event comes from the memorial's own account, from Belarusian official outlets and from testimony given in Soviet trials, so the sources below are named wherever a claim rests on them.
content.h2: A village with a long paper trail
content.p: The memorial complex's history of the place says nobody knows when Khatyn was founded, but that it first appears in writing in the middle of the sixteenth century. In July 1551 King Sigismund Augustus, who was also Grand Duke of Lithuania, granted Minsk's elder Vasily Tyshkevich the right to buy land at Khatyn and two neighbouring settlements from Tatars who had served as soldiers there. The Tyshkevich family then held the estate for more than 350 years. In 1566 Khatyn was assigned to the Catholic chapter of Vilnius.

The same account records that a wooden church of the Greek Catholic (Uniate) rite was built in the late eighteenth century and consecrated on 6 November 1794. After the abolition of the Uniate church in 1839 it became Orthodox. Population figures give the scale of the place: 63 peasants in 1816, 87 residents in 1909. In 1935 its people joined the collective farm named Red Star. By 1943, according to a German-language retelling that quotes the writer Wassil Bykow, it consisted of 26 farmsteads.
content.h2: The ambush and the order of events
content.p: Early on the morning of 22 March, Soviet partisans fired on a German vehicle on the road about 6 km from Khatyn. The memorial says a German officer was killed. A German-language retelling published in 2016 names him as Hans Welke, commander of a company of the 118th police battalion and an Olympic champion of 1936, and says the vehicle was fired on at a crossroads on the roads between Pleshinitsy and Logoisk and between Kozyri and Khatyn. The villagers, the memorial says, knew nothing of the ambush.

The same retelling says that local police then summoned a special unit, the battalion of SS Sturmbannführer Oskar Dirlewanger, and that Ukrainian members of the punitive detachment shot a group of local forest workers they had arrested on the way. That account is polemical in tone and is not corroborated by the other pages opened here, so it should be read as one writer's version. It also says the 118th battalion had been formed in Kiew in 1942, mainly from Ukrainian nationalists and from men from western regions, and that its men swore an oath to Hitler. In its telling, the Soviet leadership long avoided publishing the battalion's membership so as not to burden what it called the fraternal Ukrainian people.

The memorial's version of the massacre is detailed. The village was surrounded and the inhabitants, from the old to babes in arms, were driven from their houses to a shed at the edge of the settlement. The sick were pulled from their beds with rifle butts. Among the families named are Joseph and Anna Baranovsky with their nine children, Alex and Alexandra Novitsky with seven, and Kazimir and Elena Iotko with seven, the youngest a boy of one. Vera Yaskevich was driven in with her seven-week-old son. A girl, Lena Yaskevich, tried to flee to the woods and was overtaken and killed in front of her father. Two outsiders who happened to be in Khatyn that day, Anton Kunkevich of Yurkovichi and Kristina Slonskaja of Kameno, also died.

Once everyone was inside, the memorial says, the door was locked, the shed was covered with straw, benzine was poured on it and it was lit. The doors gave way under the weight of the crowd. People whose clothes were on fire ran out and were cut down by machine-gun fire. The German-language retelling gives a similar sequence, in which police around the shed laid out straw, poured fuel, set it alight and opened fire when the walls began to burn and collapse.

That retelling quotes testimony from a former member of the battalion. The source does not say where or when the testimony was given. The witness describes an interpreter named Lukowitsch bringing people out of their houses, a machine gun placed in front of the closed door, and Lukowitsch and a German setting the roof and straw alight. He describes the order to fire when the door fell in, and says a man he names as Meleshko pushed aside a gunner whose sights were wrongly set and took the machine gun himself. He recalls seeing a six-year-old boy run from the fire, his clothes burning, and fall under a shot from an officer, perhaps Kerner or Vasiura, though he said he did not know. He also remembers that 15 cows from Khatyn were taken to the battalion.

Sources do not agree on how many survived. The German-language retelling says one person lived, the blacksmith Iosif Kaminsky, 56 years old, who came to late at night with the lifeless body of his son beneath him. The boy had been badly wounded in the stomach and died in his father's arms. The memorial calls Kaminsky the only adult witness, and names five children as survivors: Volodia Yaskevich, aged 12, who ran for it and hid, and his sister Sonia, who hid; Sasha Zhelobkovich; seven-year-old Viktor Zhelobkovich, whose mother Anna covered him with her body as she fell; and 12-year-old Anton Baranovsky, wounded in the leg and taken for dead. Two girls, Maria Fedorovich and Yulia Klimovich, crawled to the woods and were found by villagers of Khvorosteny, but the memorial says that village was later burned too and they were killed. The injured children were taken to an orphanage at Pleshinitsy, where they grew up after the war.

The 2013 sb.by article, by a journalist who had known Volodia Yaskevich adds that he fell into a potato pit while being shot at, and stayed there until the attackers left. He died in September 2008. Kaminsky had built himself a house at Kozyri so as to live near Khatyn, and when he felt his strength going he handed it to Yaskevich.
content.h2: Counting the dead and the villages
content.p: The death toll of 149 is stated by the memorial and by the sb.by article, which also names 600-plus settlements across Belarus destroyed with their inhabitants. The German-language retelling says 149, with 76 children in one place and 75 in another. A scholarly article by Veranika Laputska likewise gives 149 Belarusians killed. The retelling's closing note says 5,295 settlements in Belarus were razed, 628 of them together with their people, and that more than 2.2 million people died under the occupation.

Belarus has since revised the national figures. The memorial states that a criminal case under Article 127 of the Criminal Code, opened by the Prosecutor General's Office in April 2021, has confirmed the destruction of at least 12,348 settlements, up from 9,200, and that 288 villages met the same fate as Khatyn, up from 186. Its English text gives different figures for the same investigation, at least 12,868 settlements and at least 290 villages. A law on the genocide of the Belarusian people was adopted on 5 January 2022. These totals are the Belarusian authorities' own, and the two versions on the memorial's page do not match.

Laputska writes that Vasyl Meleshko and Hryhorii Vasiura, other members of the 118th battalion, were tried in 1975 and 1986 respectively and both sentenced to death in a Soviet court. The name of Vladimir Katriuk had come up at both trials. Laputska describes him as having allegedly carried out atrocities in Belarus, including at Khatyn, and notes that he was never prosecuted and died in Canada in 2015.

The lawyer David Matas, speaking in 2012, said Belarus had released the records of the 1986 Vasiura trial in March 2008 and that, in his reading, they showed Katriuk had been a commander of a platoon of the battalion and personally fired a machine gun on the unarmed villagers. By his account the Canadian Federal Court ruled in Katriuk's favour in June 2009 in a case over his citizenship, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld that in November 2010, and B'nai Brith Canada asked the government in June 2011 to reconsider. Matas said no answer had arrived. Matas himself notes that the Federal Court judge, Mr Justice Nadon, found in 1999 that Katriuk had been a member of the battalion and took part in its activities in Belarus, including anti-partisan operations, but that on the evidence then before him he would not conclude that Katriuk himself committed or took part in war crimes. Katriuk's own account is not in the pages opened here.

In January 1966 the Central Committee of the Belarusian Communist Party decided to build a memorial at Khatyn, meant to stand for hundreds of destroyed Belarusian villages. A competition was announced in March 1967 and won by the architects Y. Gradov, V. Zankovich and L. Levin with the sculptor S. Selikhanov. Levin remembered the team's idea of marking each lost house with the base of a frame and raising chimney-shaped obelisks, and then, standing in the silent field, hearing a lark sing and concluding that the place needed sound.

Granite came from Ukraine and white marble from Russia, and the memorial says the whole country contributed building material. The first part opened in 1968. A torch lit at the Eternal Fire in Minsk's Victory Square was carried to the site, where Kaminsky and A. Zhelobkovich, both described as witnesses of the tragedy, spoke to a crowd of many thousands. The sb.by article says 36 million people have visited since. The memorial lists delegations from abroad and from Russian regions among recent visitors, including groups in July and August 2026.
